question: What happens to a finale that begins and ends slowly?
intro: The quartet ends slowly. A long Adagio, whose inner parts murmur in repeated sixteenths, gives way to a fifty-second Presto and then returns, shorter, to fade out. Shulman hears an experiment that looks ahead to Beethoven’s late quartets.

sections.label: Adagio · C major, with a turn to E♭ and C minor
Adagio returns
sections.mNote: Adagio returns, shorter, and fades to a pianissimo close

cues.title: A finale that starts slow
cues.text: Instead of a brisk, witty finale Haydn writes another Adagio, with a fast Presto in the middle. Shulman says two slow movements shift the quartet’s balance and emotional weight, and compares the experiment to Beethoven’s late quartets and even Bruckner and Mahler.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s programme note, last paragraph on Op. 54 No. 2 (https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf); the score is headed Finale, Adagio, with Presto and a returning Adagio marked (IMSLP #05812, pp. 193, 196, 198).

cues.title: Two violins together
cues.text: In the opening strain the two violins play the phrases together while the viola and cello move beneath them. The Adagio is built from short phrases and their answers, not one long melody.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #05812, p. 193) shows the two violins playing the phrases together in the opening bars, with moving viola and cello parts. The report shows a level of about −11 to −13 dB from 0:00 to 0:20 and −20.7 dB at 0:25; no phrase is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A hush, then the same again
cues.text: Around 0:30 the sound almost stops, the quietest moment of the opening minute, and at about 0:36 the opening music begins again. The quartet observes the repeat sign, so the Adagio’s first section is heard twice.
cues.evidence: The quietest windows include 0:30 (−31.3 dB, no detected attacks). A recurrence analysis matches 2.5–32.0 s with 38.0–67.5 s (mean chroma similarity 0.98, no transposition). The score has repeat signs in the opening Adagio (IMSLP #05812, p. 193); bars are not aligned.

cues.title: A murmur in the second ending
cues.text: After the repeat, the second ending brings a new texture: the second violin and viola repeat the same pitches in fast sixteenth notes, while the first violin plays short phrases over a moving cello counterline. The murmur keeps the slow tempo from stalling.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #05812, pp. 193–194) shows repeated sixteenth notes in violin II and viola from the second ending. A recurrence analysis matches 2.5–32.0 s with 38.0–67.5 s, which places the repeat of the opening strain; the second ending follows it, and its first bar is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Settling on G major, twice
cues.text: From about 1:20 the harmony favours G major, the dominant. The same stretch is played twice, at about 1:15 and again at 1:52, so the second strain’s settling on G is heard a second time before the music moves on.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 74.5–106.0 s with 112.5–144.0 s (similarity 0.94, no transposition). Local key reads G major at 1:20–1:45 (r 0.83–0.94) and 2:00–2:30; boundaries at 1:04 (0.55) and 1:22 (0.64). Key estimates confirm a region, not a chord.

cues.title: A Tel Aviv concert series
cues.text: The film behind this audio was posted by the Tel Aviv Museum of Art’s music channel, and its description credits Ilan Rechtman as music director of the concert series and Gilad Shabani for the video. The Danish String Quartet had borne that name since 2008, when its cellist joined.
cues.evidence: The YouTube description (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dGgmFFMFICc) gives the series’ music director and the video credit; Wikipedia’s Danish String Quartet article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_String_Quartet) dates the name to 2008, when Fredrik Schøyen Sjölin joined.

cues.title: Three cities, within two years
cues.text: The quartets reached print quickly. IMSLP records the first publication as Sieber in Paris in 1789, and further editions from Longman & Broderip in London and Hummel in Amsterdam, both undated and put at about 1790. Haydn’s reach by then was European.
cues.evidence: IMSLP’s page for String Quartets, Op. 54 (https://imslp.org/wiki/String_Quartets,_Op.54_(Haydn,_Joseph)) gives 1789 Paris, Sieber as the first publication; the page for Hob. III:57 lists the Hummel and Longman & Broderip prints with dates in square brackets, so the dating is approximate.

cues.title: A darker turn
cues.text: Around 2:40 the harmony swings to A minor for about fifteen seconds before the C major returns. A boundary just before marks the change.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 2:32 (novelty 0.86); local key reads A minor at 2:40–2:50 (r 0.71, 0.81, 0.69) and C major at 2:55 (0.84). The estimate is of a key region, not a chord.

cues.title: A loud C major, then minor
cues.text: Around 3:30 the Adagio reaches one of its loudest moments in clear C major. Within ten seconds the estimates turn to C minor: the key that coloured the slow movement returns.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows include 3:30 (−9.9 dB, C major r 0.97); boundaries at 3:24 (0.67) and 3:38 (0.70); the key estimate is C minor at 3:40–3:50 (r 0.86–0.91).

cues.title: The strongest boundary
cues.text: At 3:52 comes the strongest boundary of the whole movement. Beyond it, estimates pass through A♭ major to E♭ major, the relative major of C minor, and hold there for about twenty-five seconds. The score has a section under a three-flat key signature in this Adagio.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 3:52 (novelty 1.00), following a quiet window at 3:50 (−26.9 dB); local keys read A♭ major at 3:55 and E♭ major at 4:00–4:20 (r 0.87–0.93). The score’s three-flat stretch (IMSLP #05812, p. 195) is compatible with this region but not aligned to it.

cues.title: Back through G minor to the dominant
cues.text: The E♭ stretch ends at about 4:25. The key estimate passes G minor and C minor, then lands on G major by 4:50. The Adagio ends hushed, on a held chord, ready for the Presto.
cues.evidence: Local keys read G minor at 4:25–4:30, C minor at 4:35–4:45 and G major at 4:50–4:55 (r 0.87–0.88); level is −29.3 dB at 4:55. The score shows pp and a fermata at the end of the Adagio (p. 196).

cues.title: The Presto
cues.text: At 5:00 the Presto bursts in: detected attacks rise from almost none to five or six a second, and the level jumps by about twenty decibels. The key is C major, and the music is quick, short-breathed and full of accents.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −29.3 dB at 4:55 to −10.6 dB at 5:00; attack density rises from 1.6 to 5.6 per second; boundary at 5:00 (0.56); local key reads C major (r 0.89) at 5:00. The score marks Presto after the Adagio’s fermata (p. 196).

cues.title: Listen for the pauses
cues.text: The Presto’s opening strain is marked for a repeat, and the score also marks general pauses, G.P., when all four players stop together. Listen for the silences between the brisk figures: they matter as much as the notes.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #05812, pp. 196–197) marks repeat signs at the opening of the Presto and G.P. twice in it. The report shows the loudest windows at 5:40 and 5:45 and a quiet window at 5:35 (−25.2 dB); no repeat or pause is timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Two dates for one concert
cues.text: The Commons file dates this recording 24 July 2015, but that is the day the concert film was posted on YouTube. According to the video’s description the performance itself was in May, at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
cues.evidence: The YouTube page (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dGgmFFMFICc) shows the upload date 24 July 2015 and a description giving May 2015; the Commons file page gives 2015-07-24 as the date. An upload date is not a session date.

cues.title: The Adagio comes back
cues.text: The Presto ends on loud chords with a fermata, and the Adagio returns with its opening gesture. The level at the return, about −12 dB, matches the movement’s opening, but fewer than twenty bars remain before the end.
cues.evidence: Level is −28.0 dB at 5:50, then −10.7 dB at 5:55 and −12.4 dB at 6:00, against −12.3 dB at 0:00. A recurrence analysis matches the opening material (4.5–25.0 s) with 358.5–379.0 s (offset 354 s, similarity 0.95). The score marks Adagio after the Presto’s final fermata, with fewer than twenty bars left to Fine (printed p. 198).

cues.title: Fading to the end
cues.text: The final minute contains F major visits, a last C major, and a gradual fade to pianissimo. The marked Fine arrives quietly: the quartet stops by evaporating, not by closing with an emphatic chord.
cues.evidence: Local key reads F major at 6:35–6:40 and 6:55–7:00, C major at 6:45–6:50 and 7:05; the quietest windows are 7:10 and 7:15 (−34.2 and −34.8 dB). The score shows pp and Fine at the end (p. 198); the last chord is not timed.

transitions.title: A fermata, then the Presto
transitions.how: The Adagio ends hushed, pp, on a chord under a fermata; the key signature, three flats in the preceding stretch, is cancelled. The Presto then starts in C major at mezzo-forte with the violins moving together over off-beat cello notes. No linking passage joins the two: the fermata supplies the pause, and the sudden change of speed and sound makes the break.
transitions.evidence: Level rises from −29.3 dB at 4:55 to −10.6 dB at 5:00, attack density from 1.6 to 5.6 per second, and the boundary is at 5:00 (0.56). The fermata, pp, cancelling naturals and the Presto marking are read from the score (IMSLP #05812, pp. 195–196).

transitions.title: Loud chords, then the Adagio again
transitions.how: The Presto ends on repeated sforzando chords, then forte, and a final chord held under a fermata. The Adagio follows, marked as such, with the movement’s opening gesture of a short note, rests and a grace-note figure. The finale’s two slow outer sections are thus joined to a fast centre by a pause at each end, and the second Adagio is much shorter than the first.
transitions.evidence: The loudest windows are 5:40 (−9.1 dB) and 5:45 (−7.8 dB); level is −28.0 dB at 5:50, then −10.7 dB at 5:55, and a recurrence analysis finds the opening material again from about 354 s. The score shows sf chords, a final fermata chord and the word Adagio (IMSLP #05812, printed p. 198); the opening gesture’s resemblance to bar 1 is visible but not aligned in time.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
